Based on my research into the ICILS 2023 International Report, I was able to find references to **Table 2.2** which is located on **page 73** of the report. This table presents data from the ICILS 2023 National Contexts Survey regarding how Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) and Computational Thinking (CT) education are implemented across different countries at different ISCED levels.

The table includes three response categories:
- Compulsory to teach
- **Available but not compulsory to teach**
- Not taught

According to the search results, **CIL and CT education were reported to be more prevalent in secondary schooling than in primary schooling (ISCED 1)** according to Table 2.2.

Unfortunately, I was unable to access the full PDF of the ICILS 2023 International Report directly due to file size limitations (the document exceeded download limits), so I could not retrieve the specific country-by-country breakdown showing which countries had the most "Available but not compulsory to teach" categories at the ISCED 1 (primary school) level for both CIL and CT.

To answer your question accurately, you would need to consult **Table 2.2 on page 73 of the ICILS 2023 International Report: An International Perspective on Digital Literacy**, which would show the complete dataset of all 35 participating education systems and their responses for both CIL and CT at ISCED level 1, allowing you to identify which countries had the highest number of subjects categorized as "Available but not compulsory to teach."

## Abstract

This chapter provides an overview of national and school contexts shaping computer and information literacy (CIL) and computational thinking (CT) education in countries participating in the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS) 2023. The chapter presents data relevant to ICILS Research Question 2 for both CIL and CT: How is CIL/CT education implemented across countries, and what aspects of schools and countries are related to students’ CIL/CT? The chapter draws on data from national study centers, school principals, and ICT coordinators to explore the integration of CIL and CT within education systems and curricula, emphasizing differences across primary and secondary schooling. The chapter highlights the prevalence of CIL as a curricular focus, its frequent compulsory status, and its stronger alignment with learning goals compared to CT. It also examines national policies and resources influencing CIL and CT education, including ICT infrastructure, teacher training, and strategies to address the digital divide. School-level factors, such as ICT resources and responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, are explored, revealing varied implementation practices. Overall, the chapter underscores the complex interplay between systemic structures and local practices in fostering digital competencies among students.

**Chapter Highlights** Data collected from International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS) national study centers, school principals, and information and communication technology (ICT) coordinators suggest that the characteristics of education systems varied considerably across the ICILS 2023 participating countries.

As reported by ICILS national study centers:

* In teaching programs across countries, computer and information literacy (CIL) was included slightly more than computational thinking (CT) at all levels of schooling (Table [2.2]).

* CIL and CT education were more prevalent in secondary schooling than in primary schooling (Table [2.2]).

* CIL was more frequently compulsory than CT in countries where both were included in the curriculum at a given education level (Table [2.2]).

* The elements with the greatest representation in national plans and policies across countries include:

  * Aspects of ICT learning:

  * _The development of information literacy_

  * _ICT-based skills in critical thinking, collaboration, and communication_ (Appendix B, Table [B.1])

  * Resources:

  * _Internet connectivity_

  * _The provision of computer equipment and other ICT resources_

  * _Support for teachers in using computer equipment and other ICT resources in their work_ (Appendix B, Table [B.2])

  * Approaches to support student learning:

  * _Pre-service and in-service teacher education_ (Appendix B, Table [B.3])

  * Plans and programs:

  * _Professional development for teachers’ pedagogical use of ICT_

  * _Reduction of the digital divide between groups of students_

  * _Provision of ICT resources and digital learning materials_

  * _The development of ICT competencies in students_ (Appendix B, Table [B.4])

* A broad range of aspects of CIL were strongly represented in curricula across countries, although there was some variation in the degree to which these aspects were associated with learning goals (Table [2.3]).

* Aspects of CT were well represented in curricula across countries, although less so than the representation of CIL. The degree of explicit representation of CT and the association of CT with learning goals was lower than for CIL (Table [2.4]).

* There was considerably less emphasis on expectations that CIL and CT skills be assessed when compared to their emphases in curricula across countries (Appendix B, Table [B.5]).

## 2.1 Introduction

The contextual framework within the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS) assessment framework provides a conceptual structure to support the interpretation and analysis of the ICILS data, in particular the data associated with student proficiency in computer and information literacy (CIL) and computational thinking (CT) (Rožman et al. [2024]. Contextual framework. In J. Fraillon & M. Rožman (Eds.), IEA international computer and information literacy study 2023 assessment framework (pp. 45–55). Springer. 
  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-61194-0_4
  
  ")). Similar to the two previous cycles of ICILS, the conceptual structure provided within the framework posits that CIL and CT are developed within four levels of influence: the _wider community_, the _school/classroom_, the _home_, and finally the individual characteristics of _the student_. Furthermore, aspects of each level can be classified either as _antecedents_ (external contextual factors that indirectly affect the ways in which learning takes place) and _processes_ (contextual factors that directly affect the ways in which learning takes place) (Rožman et al.
